query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a nanometer‐scale, ALD‐deposited mixed Ce–Zr oxide overlayer on a near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst will enhance low-temperature oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons, improve resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO, and retard degradation (e.g., sintering and phase change) during aging, all while maintaining low platinum-group-metal usage.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst alloy synthesized by conventional methods, containing trace platinum-group metals and active elements such as Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt.
generation.intervention: A uniform, 2–3 nm thick Ce–Zr oxide coating deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD) onto the catalyst surface.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust comprising CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO at temperatures from 150 °C to 600 °C, combined with accelerated thermal and chemical aging cycles designed to mimic a full vehicle lifetime exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal Ce–Zr oxide overlayer that interacts with the catalyst surface, creating active oxygen vacancies and physically mitigating sintering or poisoning species adsorption.
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer promotes oxygen vacancy formation and redox cycling at lower temperatures, enhancing catalytic oxidation while acting as a barrier that minimizes sintering and protects active sites from poisoning by H2O and NO. This surface stabilization is expected to maintain catalytic performance over prolonged aging.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the coated catalyst will exhibit a lower ignition (light-off) temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation (targeting operation below 150 °C), improved retention of activity in the presence of typical exhaust poisons, and reduced degradation over accelerated aging tests.
generation.baseline: The uncoated, near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst with minimal platinum-group metals.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to be effective under regulated automotive exhaust conditions; however, its benefit may be limited under extreme or highly variable operating conditions beyond typical transient and low-temperature regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness and precise Ce–Zr composition required for maximum performance enhancement are uncertain, as are potential interactions with minor alloying elements under diverse real-world exhaust chemistries.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples using identical catalyst preparation protocols. Apply the Ce–Zr overlayer via ALD to one set while leaving the other set uncoated. Expose both to simulated automotive exhaust gas mixtures containing CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO under controlled temperatures (150–600 °C) and run accelerated aging cycles mimicking lifetime operation.
measurements: Determine light-off temperatures and conversion efficiencies for CO and hydrocarbons before and after aging (using temperature-programmed oxidation/reaction tests).
Monitor poisoning resistance by comparing activity retention in the presence of H2O and NO.
Perform post-aging structural characterization (TEM, XRD) to assess sintering or phase degradation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated catalyst does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in light-off temperature (e.g., improvement below 150 °C), or if its activity and structural integrity deteriorate more than those of the uncoated catalyst under the same aging and poisoning conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
